Sufficient Grace
sŭf-fĭsh´ĕnt grās
n. phrase (the Lord's answer to Paul's thorn: grace enough for the affliction, with the affliction left in place)
Greek arkei soi he charis mou — my grace suffices for thee. The verb arkeo means to be enough, to ward off want; it is the word behind content in Hebrews 13:5 and the root of the English autarky.

Biblical Definition

Sufficient grace is the Lord's reply to a prayer He declined: “there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me… For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:7–9). Paul's response reorganises his whole valuation: “Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me… for when I am weak, then am I strong” (2Co 12:9–10). The same sufficiency is promised for giving: “God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work” (2Co 9:8). And Hebrews sets the time: “grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sufficient as enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants; competent; and grace as the free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from Him, and the divine influence that renews the heart and sustains the believer.

SUFFICIENT, a. Enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants; competent; as provision sufficient for the family.

My grace is sufficient for thee. 2 Cor. 12.

GRACE, n. Favor; good will; kindness; disposition to oblige another.

2. Appropriately, the free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.

3. Favorable influence of God; divine influence or the influence of the spirit, in renewing the heart and restraining from sin.

Key Scripture

2Co 12:7 — "And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure."

2Co 12:9 — "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

2Co 12:10 — "Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong."

2Co 9:8 — "And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work:"

Heb 4:16 — "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."

Modern Corruption

The thorn is treated as the problem and grace as the solution that should remove it, and the text records the thorn staying.

expand to see more

The passage is more uncomfortable than its famous sentence. Paul had a thorn — he never says what — and calls it a messenger of Satan sent to buffet him, and prays three times for it to go, and it does not go. What he receives instead is a sentence, and the sentence is the whole doctrine: my grace is sufficient for thee. Not my grace will remove it. Any account of sufficient grace that expects the thorn to be withdrawn as evidence of the grace has reversed the passage; the grace was proved by the thorn remaining and Paul continuing.

The reason given is the part that offends the modern instinct most: my strength is made perfect in weakness. Perfected, completed, brought to its full working — in the exact place where the man has run out. Paul's response is not resignation but a reorganised accounting, and its verbs are startling: most gladly will I rather glory in my infirmities, I take pleasure in infirmities, reproaches, necessities, persecutions, distresses. He is not pretending they do not hurt; he has discovered what they are for. The thorn was given, he says — twice — lest I should be exalted above measure, after being caught up to the third heaven. The affliction was the antidote to the revelation.

Hebrews 4:16 supplies the timing and it is the practical half of the doctrine: grace to help in time of need. The sufficiency is not a reservoir issued in advance so that a man can inspect it and feel secure; it is delivered at the point of need, in the quantity the need requires, and not before. That is why the anxious question — could I bear it if that happened? — has no answer now and is not meant to. The grace for a trial is issued with the trial. Second Corinthians 9:8 extends the same principle to money, and its piling of all is deliberate: all grace, always, all sufficiency, all things, every good work.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek arkeo (G714), to suffice, be enough; skolops (G4647), a thorn, stake; teleioo (G5048), to perfect, complete; autarkeia (G841), sufficiency.

expand to see more

Greek arkei soi (G714) — is sufficient for thee; 2 Corinthians 12:9, and arkeo of contentment, Hebrews 13:5, 1 Timothy 6:8.

Greek skolops te sarki (G4647) — a thorn in the flesh; 2 Corinthians 12:7 only.

Greek pasan autarkeian (G841) — all sufficiency; 2 Corinthians 9:8, 1 Timothy 6:6.

Usage

"“I besought the Lord thrice” — and the thorn stayed."

"“My strength is made perfect in weakness” — completed, where the man ran out."

"“Grace to help in time of need” — issued with the trial, not before."
